newsitem.title: GERMANY: German shares hold records, but outlook seen shaky.
newsitem.headline: German shares hold records, but outlook seen shaky.

text.p: German shares held up at their record high levels on Thursday afternoon, but dealers bemoaned overall weak trading volumes and were divided on whether the market's bull run can or should continue.

Its high levels reinforced by Bunds' gains after the afternoon's U.S. data, the 30-share IBIS DAX index was up 6.67 points at 2,669.77 points at 1306 GMT, little changed from the mid-afternoon floor session close at 2,666.55.
Some dealers warned of impending vertigo.
"People are starting to get cold feet. I really think we have shot up too quickly," said one Frankfurt dealer.
Some dealers predicted that the market was due for a correction, with one forecasting a drop of as much as 2.5 percent to 2,600 points over the next few days.
"That would give us breathing space. Fundamentals here in Germany are not supporting these levels," he said.
Others said the market needed to consolidate at current levels or a little below.

Trading was focused on individual stocks still viewed as a good buy, such as pharmaceuticals group Schering AG which on Wednesday predicted a higher than expected dividend payout of two marks per share in 1996.
Schering was up 1.85 marks at 119 marks in afternoon trade.
A solid plus for the market was the firm dollar, trading around 1.52 marks in the afternoon. A strong dollar is viewed as crucial for Germany's export-driven industries like cars and chemicals.
Chemical shares were generally ahead in later trade, offsetting weakness in the financial sector, which was hurt by news that Moody's is reviewing ratings of Deutsche Bank, the country's largest.
Deutsche was down 73 pfennigs at 72.12 marks in afternoon electronic trade.
Retail group Metro AG, one of this week's newcomers to the bluechip DAX index, was up 3.10 marks at 139.60 after it posted well-received first-half profits.
The group said its operating profit rose to 181 million marks in the period from 48 million -- a figure analysts viewed neutrally, but were relieved to find no bad surprises.
